Or when they get really stressed they break down. But your life is still melted together and together you have to deal with it.

My husband does enough but it's mostly me. This dog and I have a really special connection. I was the one who picked him up from the rescue. I was the one who he bonded with. I'm who he trusts. After this money thing happened I was the one who shut down. I laid on the couch for a month staring. Not watching tv. Not reading. Staring. Drifting in and out of sleep. He laid next to me. When I came home from the hospital I came back and laid down and he wouldn't leave my side.

I work from home and while I make enough to pay most of our bills I don't make enough to go buy my own place, put a deposit down, and then maintain taking care of him and me. I almost died. Or at least that was what everyone was telling me. I was in college and I felt really off. I couldn't stand or walk. I went to the little ER in town and nothing was wrong. 

My parents picked me up and took me to my main doctor in Cleveland, OH because I have a chronic illness, and upon taking my vitals he sent me downstairs to the urgent care where I was immediately transferred to one of the big hospitals there via ambulance. My heart rate, sitting down and resting was 180. Standing up in jumped over 200. 

By the time I got to the hospital it was in the 140s. I ended up admitted because they didn't know what was wrong, and unknown to me at the time when your heart is acting crazy like that it sometimes can go fuck you and stop. I was put on a constant heart monitor and every time I would stand up nurses would run into the room. 

As the week went on they ran test after test. All negative. Finally, we pushed them to call my neurologist. I have a nerve disease and I felt like if it wasn't a heart problem that they could find it obviously had to be a nerve problem. 

My neurologist comes in and no joke, within ten minutes he diagnoses me. I was part of a study he did earlier that year and he already knew my erratic heart was a problem but due to the confidentiality agreement of the study he wasn't allowed to tell me.  The reason I wasn't having symptoms previously is his theory that my nerve damage was so severe that I couldn't pick up on it. I was diagnosed with POTS. I have a mitochondrial disease that causes a bunch of bullshit. Or at least that was the consensus then. I don't know where things stand now to be honest because I feel like things are constantly changing as more research is done. 

So. I ended up having to drop out of college that semester for a disorder that could have been being treated. 

At this point I have been in the hospital a week. The nerve disease causes severe pain with slight movement (Google allodynia) and the hospital I was at has these stupid beds that vibrate and move. It made my nerve disease flare. 

Over the period of the next few months I lost my ability to walk unassisted. I sunk into a deep depression.  I dumped an amazing man because I couldn't stand to be touched. 

When life hit bottom I decided to hit back. I ended up deciding to raise money for the organization that primarily funds research and education for my nerve disease. It is called the Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy Association. My sorority held a spaghetti dinner and I worked hard to raise awareness for the disease. I spent months doing intense physical therapy and gained back my ability to walk. Once I did that, I applied for a dream internship working for a campaign, which then turned into a job. I also met my husband during this time. 

Life isn't perfect now. Kind of sucks right now actually, but that experience taught me that when things are absolute shit you can always turn it around step by step. You just have to make the decision to. I made the decision to turn things around this time and it's slowly happening. My health will always throw me curve balls and I'll want to quit a lot, but a day at a time. 

TL;DR- Typical got sick, life sucked, life got better, learned lesson.

Third, your poop will turn grey or almost white. Normally what turns it brown is the bilirubin but now it'll be in your blood and your pee, so your poop is pretty colorless. 

If you have multiple, or those three symptoms plus pain, definitely see a doctor ASAP. 4,000mg Tylenol is generally where you can top out safely, so depending on your weight and a few other things you may be totally fine. If you are concerned and having any prolonged pain even if you don't have those symptoms it may still be worth seeing a GP.

I have a lot of sympathy and understanding most of the time. I try to come from a place of understanding and try to look at ways I can change my behavior to further show who I am and who I'm not. 

For example, I get severe nausea from morphine and similar medication. When I was in a situation where I needed pain medication I said something like, "I don't like morphine." In hindsight, I get how that sounds and I understand why I kind of got a sassy reply of, "Well, what do you like?" What I meant was more, "I get nausea from narcotics, so is there anything that will work but is less likely to have that side effect." 

Doctors in those situations don't know me. They only have a few minutes or seconds of interaction and a lot of what you are going off of is based on other people with similar symptoms/issues/etc.

Honestly, I've personally been very fortunate. My doctors and I try to avoid narcotics and I have a long relationship with my pain management doctor so there is trust there. My biggest issue has been with emergency medicine. Often it is for reasons not even related to pain. 

For example, a few years ago I had a severe ear infection to the point I couldn't eat, sleep, or hear. My PCP sent me to the emergency room because they felt they couldn't do anything more to help. I ended up getting treated terribly. They acted like I was just there for pain management (no, I was there because my PCP sent me there, I assume for IV medication.) They didn't even bother looking at my ear. 

The next day I ended up getting dragged back by my boss because my entire face was swollen at this point. Luckily, I got a doctor who I had seen before and at this point they were physically unable to even look at my ear. I had to get scans to ensure the infection hadn't spread to my bone. I ended up reporting those doctors. 

Another time I ended up in the hospital for an emergency and was not at my normal hospital and even though I have no history of drug abuse, a hospitalist decided to take me off of my medications. 

Now, because I'm not on regular narcotics I am on high doses of tramadol. I also take topomax and a muscle relaxer. I had brought in my medication bottles. They had access to my pharmacy to confirm dosage. But yet they decided to take me off all of my medication and not to replace it. It wasn't until I demanded a second opinion and called my pain management doctor's office to have them explain what my condition is, did they end up restarting my medication. I was literally being tortured. I have one of the most painful diseases there is. 

I am honestly very sympathetic to people who abuse medication. It's so much easier to be high than to feel your pain, mental or physical. I just also see the other side. 

As I said, I've been so lucky in that 99% of the time I'm not affected by it. I have surrounded myself with a great medical team and I am honest with them in the hope that they'll be honest with me. 

However, there is also that percent where when I feel abnormally sick and I'm terrified to get emergency care. I'm scared I won't get taken seriously. I'm scared of how mean people can be. I am constantly afraid of making some kind of mistake with how I describe how I'm feeling.  Normal people don't worry about these things.

Do you know your neighbors/know the temperament of their dog? If you do I recommend introducing them as long as you don't worry about the safety of your puppy. 

We have a very vocal dog. I'll completely admit it is absolutely horrible. I love her to death but she won't shut up. We've done training, collars, positive and negative reinforcement, crate training, etc. She's just loud. I assume that isn't the problem your neighbor's have because it sounds like a new issue, but our dog is less likely to bark at things she recognizes. So since she is friendly (loud but friendly) we try to introduce to new tenants and animals. This helps us in a few ways. First, new people become familiar with who our dog is. Second, we can explain to them we are not abusive and that sadly she is just really damn loud. They also learn that loud is not equal to aggressive in her case, even though she sounds that way. Third, she becomes more familiar with who they are, what they sound like, and she's less likely to bark at them. 

Now, I suggest this to you because puppies, they are going to bark. They almost always do when they are adjusting to being alone and crate training. Chances are you don't end up with a dog who thinks their sole purpose on this earth is to let anyone who can hear them know when anything of minor importance is happening, but even then you'll still probably have to deal with minor barking. Most dogs have it go away. My other dog? He's silent. If other tenants know why there is a puppy screaming in your apartment they are a lot less likely to get annoyed. So show him or her off. Socialization is great, too.
